context_blurb:
A mountain looks as if it will last forever, but it is slowly wearing away. Rain, rivers, wind and ice break rock into bits and carry the bits off, grain by grain. Over thousands and millions of years, that slow work carves out valleys, heaps up hills of sand and builds new land where a river meets the sea.

Scientists split this work into two jobs. Weathering is the breaking: rock cracks and crumbles into smaller pieces right where it sits. Erosion is the carrying: running water, wind, ice or gravity moves the pieces somewhere else. In short, weathering breaks rock up, and erosion carries it away.

Freezing water is a mighty rock-breaker. Rain trickles into cracks in rock, and when the cold comes, the water freezes. Water takes up nearly a tenth more room as ice, so the ice shoves the crack a little wider. When the ice melts, water seeps deeper, ready for the next freeze. So rock splits fastest where it freezes and thaws again and again, as on high mountains. Rock that stays frozen all year cracks far more slowly, however bitter the cold.

Living things break rock too. When a tree grows out of a crack in a rock, its roots creep down into the gap and thicken every year. Like a wedge tapped in very slowly, the roots push the crack wider until the rock splits. In loose soil, roots hold the ground in place, but in solid rock they pry it apart.

Rivers carve the land. The sand and stones in a river scrape its bed like sandpaper, cutting it a little deeper every year. Over millions of years, a river can slowly saw its way down through solid rock and leave a deep, narrow canyon with steep walls. An earthquake cracks the ground, but it does not open a canyon.

On an ordinary day a mountain stream rolls along only sand and little pebbles, but a storm can turn it into a flood that rushes far faster than usual. The faster water flows, the bigger the rocks it can push and carry, so a racing flood can sweep along boulders that sit still on a calm day. The boulders never float, because ordinary rock is two to three times as heavy as the same amount of water.

Where a river runs into the still sea, it slows down. Slow water cannot carry as much, so the river drops the mud and sand it carries. This dropping is called deposition. Over thousands of years the mud piles up into a broad, flat plain of new land at the river's mouth: a delta, named after the Greek letter delta, a triangle, the shape a delta often takes.

Wind works on dry, sandy ground. It bounces sand grains along close to the ground and drops them wherever it slows, heaping them into hills. These hills are sand dunes, built by the wind in deserts and along beaches.

Ice carves the land as well. A glacier is a huge mass of ice that creeps slowly downhill, and it carves a valley shaped like a U. Stones frozen into its bottom grind the rock as it goes. Because it scrapes a valley's sides as well as its floor, it leaves steep sides and a broad, rounded bottom. A river cuts mostly downward instead, leaving a narrower valley shaped like a V.

Glaciers, rivers and wind mostly work slowly, over thousands of years. A few changes are fast: in a landslide, gravity drags a mass of rock and soil down a steep hillside, and the quickest landslides are over in seconds or minutes. Heavy rain soaking the ground, or an earthquake shaking it, often sets one off.
